newsitem.title: UK: Med refiners mop up sweet and sour, Urals goes West.
newsitem.headline: Med refiners mop up sweet and sour, Urals goes West.

text.p: Mediterranean refiners are likely to have to pay more for sour barrels as end-Sept Urals crude dried up, with a refiner-trader rumoured to be considering moving 130,000 tonnes of end-September Urals to the Caribbean, traders and refiners said.
The deal was heard done at a strong Dated Brent -70 cents, higher than the Dated -80 cents c+f Augusta paid by a refiner for 60,000 tonnes, also c+f Augusta, on Thursday.
Traders thought the first cargo could reappear in the Med if differentials improved further.
Med traders said Urals was bid at Dated -78/80 cents a barrel against offers of Dated -85 cents. Some sellers were eyeing Dated -60 cents for early October barrels.
Med refiners say the recent surge in gas oil prices has improved their margins after several months in the doldrums. The margin on sour crude is currently put at $3.0 a barrel for Urals.
"The margin on sours has improved. It is not quite as good as Nigerian crudes but it is fairly positive," a Med refinery buyer said.
Med crude differentials have soared this week as a result of the better margins, especially for sweet, distillate-rich grades.

There was some talk that North Sea Forties and sour Flotta had moved into the Med, but this could not be confirmed. A North Sea trader confirmed a 650,000-tonne cargo of Flotta loading Oct 1-3 was sold to a Spanish refiner on Wednesday.
"Sour is tight, so Flotta is moving down to the Med," the trader said.

A broker said sweet grades were in demand in the Med for blending with sour to reduce the sulphur content of gas oil, particularly with the approach of the October 1 deadline for the European switch to 0.05 percent sulphur.
Urals sellers said this was more evidence that Med refiners were switching to other grades because of the tightness of sour crudes.

"Refiners are scrambling around for what they can find. There is no Urals and they are having to buy sweets. If you look at the strength in high sulphur fuel, there is no doubt that sour is in demand," said a trader looking to sell October Urals.
"If Flotta makes it into the Med, that is more proof that Urals has to rise further," he added.
The strong gas oil prices in Europe and the tight WTI/Brent spread have driven more than the usual amount of West African crude into the Med.

Sweet Mediterranean crudes were also benefiting from increased refiner demand. Algeria has asked for Dated Brent +70 cents for its crude, against +61 cents in September. Syria is also aiming for higher prices for its lighter grades.

One broker said the new regulation 0.05 percent sulphur diesel would make Algerian crude attractive, but that many refiners were balking at the higher price and were considering not lifting in October.
